explanations.explanation: This neuron fires whenever the model sees a “.” (or similar end‐of‐unit dot) marking sentence boundaries or abbreviations (including initials, phonetic dots, technical specs, etc.) across languages and contexts.

This neuron is basically a “structural‐boundary” detector for the period token.  It lights up on full stops that terminate short, metadata-style fragments—abbreviations (Gov., Aug.), dates/times (25. November 2008 at 02:07.), version numbers (RSS 2.0), list or section headings (Day 38.), disclaimers, headings and similar one-line items—i.e. it flags the period as a marker of a self-contained, structural segment.

1. Recognizes mentions of “stainless steel” products and related manufacturing contexts.  
2. Marks references to agile/DevOps methodologies and speed-oriented software practices.  
3. Fires on descriptions of battery-powered slow-cooker (“crock-pot”) appliances.  
4. Activates for a firm’s introduction of audit services aimed at non-profit and private sectors.  
5. Flags step-by-step mechanical assembly instructions (panel alignment, drilling, hinges).  
6. Highlights the concept of “respect” as a foundational or “glue” element in organizational culture.  
7. Indicates networking constraints and traffic-shaping configurations on routers/ISRs.  
8. Picks up on version-control merge-conflict issues caused by auto-generated index.html files.  
9. Focuses on rooting Android devices (Huawei P10), third-party apps, and custom ROMs.  
10. Calls out software release notes: upcoming version numbers, bug fixes, and preview builds.  
11. Surfaces local service advertising copy—here, fireplace installation contractors.  
12. Detects marketing advice about using infographics to boost website traffic and engagement.  
13. Identifies numismatic coin-grading terminology and preservation-state discussions.  
14. Marks plumbing service pitches emphasizing video-tech-enabled drain/sewer diagnostics.  
15. Highlights a one-day executive workshop on strategic analysis and decision-making.  
16. Activates for financial-model discussions around fee-for-service remote patient monitoring.  
17. Captures legal commentary on governmental immunity statutes and related case questions.  
18. Flags Chrome 72/WebRTC SDP “mid” attribute changes affecting browser negotiation.  
19. Notices influencer-marketing fraud discussion: fake followers vs. brand service quality.  
20. Identifies auto-body-repair shop promotions, OEM warranties, and vehicle restoration.

This neuron is a detector for “boilerplate” site‐UI language—generic instructions about user identity or site utilities (e.g. the “if you are/not … register” conditional in placeholder pages and the “follow … via RSS” feed notice in blog footers).

This neuron is essentially a “dot detector” – it lights up on the period token whenever it’s used inside or at the end of structured, “dotted” formats (abbreviations and initialisms like Jan., Inc., U.S.; decimal points in numbers like 8.5; times like 4:00; etc.).
This feature lights up on the “dot” in shorthand numeric/temporal abbreviations—e.g. month‐abbreviations (Nov. Sept. Jan.), time markers (a.m., p.m.), and numeric decimals (3.75, 5.25, $50.00).

This neuron fires on “label” tokens – the initial, often capitalized subword of a proper-noun or headline-style keyword (county names, product or module titles, disorder names, circuit types, skills, etc.) that serve as topical headings or category labels in lists and descriptions.
This neuron is essentially a “period” detector—it lights up on the full-stop token (the “.”) marking sentence endings, abbreviations, domain names, etc.

This neuron fires on subword tokens that mix in non‐letter symbols—digits, hyphens or slashes, diacritics, emoji or other punctuation—i.e. the “weird” bits in technical names, version codes, abbreviations or foreign/garbled text.

This neuron fires on the “.” that closes short all-caps or capitalized sequences used as abbreviations or labels (month names like “Jan.”/“Nov.”/“Sept.,” corporate suffixes like “Inc.,” figure or section tags like “Fig. 9.1,” initials, dateline markers, etc.), essentially signalling the period in structured, abbreviated contexts.
